claim: “possibly can be used in modal harmony with deontic can in requests for permission or action”, with [4i] Could I possibly borrow your bicycle for half an hour? and [4ii] Could you possibly come a little earlier next week?
evidence_summary: Ch. 3, p. 200 [56ii] has Can you pass the salt, please and Could you pass the salt, please: “questions about your ability are conventionally used as requests”. There [57ii] Might/Could I have a little more sugar? is labelled [deontic]. Ch. 10, p. 939 [42] separates [ability] Can you open the door from “the deontic necessity for you to do something”, and p. 940 [43] lists can you and could you as openers of ability questions.
finding: Medium confidence. The permission request in [4i] is deontic in Ch. 3 as well, but the request for action in [4ii] is an ability question there and in Ch. 10. The defence that deontic here loosely means directive force fails, since Ch. 10 [42] keeps ability and deontic necessity apart. The modal-harmony point itself stands.
proposed_wording: possibly can be used in modal harmony with deontic can in requests for permission, and with ability can in requests for action
inference: Is could in a request for action deontic?

evidence.passage: §16, p. 768. “possibly can be used in modal harmony with deontic can in requests for permission or action”
evidence.establishes: Two other chapters treat requests for action with can or could as ability questions.
